title: Stop making up reasons to be mad at your adversaries
gist: Yglesias defends Abdul El-Sayed's resurfaced 9/11 tweet as a reasonable statement of a widely-held view, then uses the controversy to diagnose a broader online pattern of circular guilt-by-association reasoning applied to political opponents.

insights.claim: A five-year-old tweet by Abdul El-Sayed saying he would mourn 9/11 victims on the anniversary but mourn the 'tragic ways' the American response went wrong the next day resurfaced online in late August 2026 after being flagged by Twitter user Eyal Yakoby, and drew hundreds of thousands of views.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Illustrates how old social-media statements resurface as attack lines in live political campaigns (here, apparently tied to Michigan Senate primary politics).
insights.quote: Abdul El-Seyed deleted this post. It would be a shame if it went viral.

insights.claim: The view that the U.S. military response to 9/11 (the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq) was ultimately unproductive and cost many civilian and soldier lives and vast sums of money is very widely held, including by the author, even though it remains politically risky to voice near the anniversary.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A reminder that mainstream elite opinion on the post-9/11 wars has shifted to viewing them as net-negative, which continues to shape how politicians frame foreign-policy restraint and military-intervention skepticism.
insights.quote: The view that the American military response to 9/11 ended up being unproductive is very widely held.
insights.locator: My sincere advice to anyone considering a run for elected office

insights.claim: Advice for anyone considering a run for elected office: never say anything thoughtful or provocative around a national day of mourning, regardless of how reasonable the underlying point is.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A practical communications-risk heuristic for evaluating political candidates' past statements and forecasting which resurfaced remarks will become liabilities.
insights.locator: My sincere advice to anyone considering a run for elected office

insights.claim: A common online political pattern is to first decide someone is an enemy, then reinterpret everything they've said through that presumption, and then treat the resulting reinterpretation as new evidence of wrongdoing — a fully circular argument that doesn't actually add information.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A generalizable lens for discounting guilt-by-association attacks in political and market-relevant reputational disputes: check whether the 'new evidence' actually stands alone or is just recycled suspicion.
insights.quote: this is an illustration of a problematic internet trend where you decide first that someone is your enemy, then read everything he says through the presumption that he’s a bad guy, and then treat this purely circular reasoning as if it’s new evidence of new wrongdoing.
insights.locator: Not to do a whole take about 9/11

insights.claim: Attacks on Abdul El-Sayed over his 9/11 tweet rest on reading it through his association with commentator Hasan Piker during the Michigan Senate primary, even though El-Sayed has specifically disavowed Piker's remarks about 9/11 and, unlike Piker, supports Western aid to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Distinguishes El-Sayed's actual policy positions (pro-Ukraine-aid) from the 'campist anti-American left' label being applied to him via association, relevant for accurately reading his political profile ahead of the Michigan Senate race.
insights.quote: he has specifically disavowed Piker’s remarks about 9/11. What’s more, El-Sayed supports Western aid to Ukraine — he is not part of the campist anti-American left, while Piker seems to be.
insights.locator: It’s true that if you want to look at the most outré things Hasan Piker has ever said

insights.claim: If a controversial figure had never made the specific statement being attacked, critics angry at them for unrelated reasons would still find something else to be mad about — meaning outrage over any single resurfaced statement often adds no real new information about the person.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A test investors/analysts can apply to political-risk headlines: ask whether the specific flagged statement is doing real evidentiary work or is just a pretext for pre-existing opposition.
insights.quote: If El-Sayed had never tweeted about 9/11, you could still be mad about the other stuff. Being mad about the tweet doesn’t add anything.
insights.locator: But that’s a fully circular argument
